title: It was a great week for innovation across the model ecosystem. We’re bringing these new models into Copilot, enabling it to take on increasingly complex work, from quick questions to delegated tasks and, increasingly, complete long-running jobs through Autopilots. [Read more]
summary: It was a great week for innovation across the model ecosystem. We're bringing these new models into Copilot, enabling it to take on increasingly complex work, from quick questions to delegated tasks and, increasingly, complete long-running jobs through Autopilots. Here's one fun example: using an Opal-powered Autopilot running on a secure Windows 365 Cloud PC, Copilot goes through a month of trail cam footage, finds every animal sighting, creates a highlight reel of the best clips, labels each one with the camera, date, and species, catalogs every sighting in a spreadsheet, builds a PowerPoint summarizing the findings, and shares everything in Teams for colleagues to review. This is the next frontier for Copilot: software that doesn't just assist with work, but can own and complete entire tasks that unfold over hours or days. Learn more about Opal, the technology powering one of these new Autopilot experiences (in Frontier rings now and coming to Copilot soon): https://lnkd.in/grsmeiNt | 304 comments on LinkedIn

This is the next frontier for Copilot: software that doesn't just assist with work, but can own and complete entire tasks that unfold over hours or days. [Satya Nadella](https://www.linkedin.com/in/satyanadella?trk=public_post_comment-text) , the trail cam demo is impressive. The hard part starts after the share to Teams. A day of autonomous work needs a named owner who checks the outcome, not only the output. Species labels in a spreadsheet look done. Wrong labels in production do not. So before an Autopilot runs for hours, I would ask three things: who reviews, what signal shows it went wrong, and who is allowed to stop it. Without that, you automated the work and outsourced the responsibility.
